\chapter{How the Body Reports}
\label{ch:ml-how-the-body-reports}
\hlchaptermodality{63}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name hunger, tiredness, pain, a cough and a fever in Malayalam.}

Complete ML-C63-fever and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[viśappŭ]{\ml{വിശപ്പ്} (viśappŭ) — hunger}

\label{lesson:ML-C63-hunger}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{cūlŭ} mean, and what did \emph{muṟaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വിശപ്പ്}}
\textbf{\ml{വിശപ്പ്}} (\emph{viśappŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}hunger\textquotedblright{}.

Native Dravidian, built off \emph{viśakkuka}, the word for going hungry — the state named from the process rather than the other way round.

Tamil reaches for a different root here, \emph{paci}, so this is one of the places where the two closest sisters part company on an everyday word.

You already have the part of the body it reports from: \emph{vayaṟŭ}, the stomach. One is the place, this is the message.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things the body reports.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{viśappŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vayaṟŭ}, then \emph{viśappŭ}, and say which of the two is a feeling
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{വിശപ്പ്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}hunger\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kṣīṇaṁ]{\ml{ക്ഷീണം} (kṣīṇaṁ) — tiredness}

\label{lesson:ML-C63-tiredness}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{viśappŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ക്ഷീണം}}
\textbf{\ml{ക്ഷീണം}} (\emph{kṣīṇaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}tiredness\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{kṣīṇa}, meaning worn away or diminished, from a root about wasting down to nothing.

In Malayalam the heavier sense has itself worn away, and the word has settled into ordinary speech for the plain tiredness of a long day.

It opens on the \ml{ക്ഷ} pair that opens \emph{kṣamikkaṇaṁ}, the sorry-word — one letter riding on another, and the second one you have met wearing it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kṣīṇaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kṣamikkaṇaṁ}, then \emph{kṣīṇaṁ}, and hear the same opening twice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{ക്ഷീണം} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}tiredness\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vēdana]{\ml{വേദന} (vēdana) — pain}

\label{lesson:ML-C63-pain}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kṣīṇaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വേദന}}
\textbf{\ml{വേദന}} (\emph{vēdana}) — \textquotedblleft{}pain\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{vedanā}, from the root \emph{vid}, to know or to feel — pain named as the thing a body knows without being told.

That root has been busy in this book. \emph{Vaidyan}, the doctor, and \emph{vidyārtthi}, the student, both grow from it: knowing, learning, healing and hurting all off one seed.

Malayalam keeps it for bodily pain first and lets the wider sense follow, so a speaker saying \ml{വേദന} is usually pointing somewhere.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vēdana}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vaidyan}, then \emph{vēdana}, and say which of the two is the reason for the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{വേദന} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}pain\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cuma]{\ml{ചുമ} (cuma) — a cough}

\label{lesson:ML-C63-cough}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vēdana} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ചുമ}}
\textbf{\ml{ചുമ}} (\emph{cuma}) — \textquotedblleft{}a cough\textquotedblright{}.

Native, and built the way the crow's name was built: the sound comes first and the word is shaped to match it.

Tamil went elsewhere for this one, to \emph{irumal}, from a root of its own — a second parting between the two sisters inside one short chapter.

It covers the single cough and the standing complaint alike, so a speaker adds a word about how long it has gone on when that matters.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cuma}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kākka}, then \emph{cuma}, and say what the making of the two words has in common
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{ചുമ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a cough\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pani]{\ml{പനി} (pani) — a fever}

\label{lesson:ML-C63-fever}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{cuma} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{പനി}}
\textbf{\ml{പനി}} (\emph{pani}) — \textquotedblleft{}a fever\textquotedblright{}.

Native Dravidian, matching Tamil \emph{paṉi} — where the same word means cold, dew and frost.

Malayalam took the shivering and let the weather go. What the two senses share is a body that cannot get warm, which is the first hour of a fever and the whole of a cold morning.

Kerala hangs the word on the season: the weeks after the monsoon breaks are fever weeks, and \ml{പനി} is the word on everybody's tongue.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the body has said its piece: hunger, tiredness, pain, a cough and a fever.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pani}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{viśappŭ}, \emph{kṣīṇaṁ}, \emph{vēdana}, \emph{cuma}, \emph{pani}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{പനി} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a fever\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
